text:
The Great Molasses Flood

January 15, 1919, began as an ordinary Wednesday in Boston's North End. After a bitter cold spell the temperature had climbed to about 40 degrees, and people were out enjoying the break in the weather. Laborers ate lunch near the waterfront, children played in the streets, and freight wagons moved along Commercial Street. Above them stood a huge steel tank, about 50 feet tall and 90 feet across, owned by the Purity Distilling Company. It held more than two million gallons of molasses, which would be turned into industrial alcohol. That alcohol was used in liquor and in munitions.

Just after half past twelve, witnesses heard a deep rumble and a rapid popping, like a machine gun. Those were the rivets holding the tank's steel plates together, shearing off one after another. Then the tank split open.

A brown wave about 25 feet high swept into the street. People often picture molasses as slow, but this wave moved at around 35 miles per hour. It carried a weight of thousands of tons, and nothing in its path could stand against it. It knocked buildings off their foundations and buckled a steel support of the elevated railway, and a train only just stopped in time. A firehouse was pushed toward the harbor and partly collapsed. Wagons, horses and people were lifted and thrown aside.

The worst part came after the wave passed. Molasses covered several blocks, waist-deep in places, and in the cold air it quickly thickened. Anyone caught in it found that the harder they struggled, the more firmly it held them. Horses sank and could not get out. Rescuers struggled to wade in, and some victims suffocated before anyone could reach them.

Help arrived fast. Cadets from a nearby training ship, the USS Nantucket, ran to the scene, followed by police, firefighters and Red Cross volunteers. They worked through the afternoon and into the night, pulling survivors out of the sticky wreckage. The search for bodies went on for days, and some were found only months later in the harbor. In all, 21 people died, among them a 10-year-old boy named Pasquale Iantosca, and about 150 were injured.

The cleanup took weeks. Crews hosed the streets with salt water from fireboats and spread sand to soak up what was left. Molasses was tracked across the city on shoes, streetcar seats and wagon wheels. The harbor ran brown for months, and for decades longtime residents said they could still smell molasses on hot summer days.

The company first blamed the disaster on anarchists, saying a bomb had destroyed the tank. Survivors and families sued, and after years of hearings a court-appointed auditor rejected that explanation. The evidence showed that the tank had been built in a hurry in 1915. Its steel was too thin for the load and was never properly tested. The tank had leaked so badly that neighbors collected the drips, and the company painted it brown to hide them. The man who oversaw its construction could not read a blueprint. In 1925 the company was held responsible and paid hundreds of thousands of dollars in settlements.

The disaster led Massachusetts, and later other states, to require that licensed engineers check and sign off on the plans for large structures. It is remembered now as a strange and almost unbelievable event. It is also a lesson about cutting corners: a tank of something as harmless as molasses killed 21 people.
